lines.text: Here's the whole idea, in four sentences.
One. A robot can only push as hard as its tires grip, about one g, and slipping wheels make odometry lie.
Two. Grip moves with the weight, turning shares it, and motors lose push as they speed up.
Three. So every loop, Acceleration Limiter caps the spin change, checks the motors, and fits it all inside the grip.
Four. The current limit stays high, as a ceiling, so the heavy wheels have room to push.
Now, check yourself. Pause after each question.
Question one. Our robot gains ten kilograms. Should traction accel change?
Not by the formula: the mass cancels. But the motor check gets weaker, because robot mass is in it.
Question two. Why not set k slip current to sixty amps, and stop slip that way?
A low limit stops the heavy back wheels from pushing harder when the front ones slip. Slower, with worse odometry.
Question three. At four meters per second, which limit matters more, grip or motors?
The motors. At four, they can add only nine point seven, just under the grip's ten.
Question four. Why does the traction check shrink a x, a y and alpha together?
So the direction doesn't change. Shrinking only one would bend the path.
Question five. Why doesn't the motor check run when the robot brakes?
When braking, back E M F helps instead of fighting. Only grip limits braking.
Now try it. In the Python simulator's Q seven limiter study, add a row with traction twelve, and run the bench.
Compare slip and odometry error with traction ten. Is a little time worth it? Then try eight.
Or in the Java simulator, set traction accel to seven, and watch the commanded velocity ramp more gently. Never go below six.
